quiz_int:1.q: The arrow marks the fine bridges that cross between neighboring cells of this epidermal layer. The core proteins of the junctions at these bridges belong to which family?
quiz_int:1.r: The bridges of the stratum spinosum are desmosomes (p. 1002). The slide labels desmosomes 'cadherins' (p. 1001) and the handout says their core proteins are desmogleins, part of the cadherin superfamily (p. 1067).
quiz_int:1.alt: High-power micrograph of polygonal epidermal cells with a yellow arrow on the border between two cells.

quiz_int:11.q: A child with albinism has a skin biopsy. Which finding is expected in the epidermis?
quiz_int:11.r: Albinism is a lack of tyrosinase activity (p. 1015): a genetic defect in tyrosinase means no melanin is made even though melanocytes are present (p. 1071).

quiz_int:12.q: A drug blocks release of the contents of lamellar granules by cells of the stratum granulosum. Which function of the epidermis is lost most directly?
quiz_int:12.r: Lamellar granules secrete lipid sheets into the intercellular space to form a barrier to desiccation (p. 1004); the slide lists them under water proofing (p. 1008).

quiz_int:13.q: Which lettered structure forms the nail plate?
quiz_int:13.r: E is the nail matrix, the part of the epidermis responsible for nail formation. The nail bed (C) supports the plate but does not contribute to its formation (p. 1074, p. 1038).
quiz_int:13.alt: Drawing of a fingertip cut lengthwise through the nail, with structures lettered A to E.

quiz_int:15.q: The arrow marks the core that is enclosed by the hair bulb. How does this core differ from the rest of the follicle?
o: It is a thickened basement membrane
It is continuous with the epidermis
It is made of hard keratin
quiz_int:15.r: The hair papilla is a dermal connective tissue core, essential for induction and maintenance of the follicle, that supplies blood and nerves (p. 1075). The slide marks it 'dermal' while the follicle itself is epidermal (p. 1040, p. 1039).
quiz_int:15.alt: Drawing of the lower end of a hair follicle cut lengthwise, with a yellow arrow on the central core at its base.

quiz_int:16.q: The arrow marks one layer of the wall of this hair follicle. With which structure is this layer continuous?
quiz_int:16.r: The arrow is on the external root sheath, which is continuous with the skin's epithelium (p. 1075, p. 1042).
quiz_int:16.alt: Color diagram of a hair follicle, its gland and muscle, with all printed labels hidden and a yellow arrow on the outer layer of the follicle wall.

quiz_int:17.q: This is a cross section of a hair follicle. What does the layer marked by the arrow do?
o: Separates the hair follicle from the dermis
Supplies blood and nerves to the hair bulb
Anchors and shapes the growing hair shaft
Makes the pigment of the hair cortex
Raises the hair during cold or fear
quiz_int:17.r: The faculty answer for this arrow is the internal root sheath (p. 1064): the rigid layer closest to the hair shaft that helps anchor and shape the growing shaft (p. 1076). The glassy membrane separates the follicle from the dermis (p. 1044).
quiz_int:17.alt: Cross section of a hair follicle with concentric layers around a central dark shaft; yellow arrow on the ring next to the shaft.

quiz_int:19.q: A man with the genetic background and androgen levels for balding loses scalp hair. What happens to the affected hairs?
o: Terminal hairs convert to vellus hairs
Vellus hairs convert to terminal hairs
Terminal hairs convert to lanugo hairs
Hair follicles disappear from the scalp
quiz_int:19.r: Balding involves conversion of scalp terminal hairs to the vellus type and requires genetic background and androgenic hormones (p. 1076, p. 1046).

quiz_int:2.q: The yellow arrow marks a layer of thick skin whose cells contain dark granules that have no membrane. These granules consist mainly of which protein?
quiz_int:2.r: The stratum granulosum holds keratohyalin granules, which have no membrane and are predominantly filaggrin, the protein that binds keratin (p. 1004, p. 1069).
quiz_int:2.alt: Micrograph of thick skin epidermis and dermal papillae with the printed labels hidden and a yellow arrow on one layer.

quiz_int:21.q: A patient loses scalp hair during chemotherapy. According to the lecture, which fast-growing cells does the drug destroy?
quiz_int:21.r: The slide labels the germinal matrix of the hair bulb: chemotherapy destroys fast growing cells, causing hair loss (p. 1040).

quiz_int:22.q: The arrow marks an encapsulated structure lying in a dermal papilla. What does it detect?
quiz_int:22.r: A Meissner's corpuscle is the light touch mechanoreceptor of the papillary layer, prominent in thick skin (p. 1032, p. 1033, p. 1073).
quiz_int:22.alt: High-power micrograph of two dermal papillae pushing up into the epidermis; a yellow arrow marks an oval structure inside one papilla.

quiz_int:23.q: This rounded structure lies deep in the dermis. Which statement about it is correct?
o: It detects light touch on the fingertips
It lies in the papillary layer of dermis
It secretes sweat onto the skin surface
It detects deep pressure and vibration
It shunts blood from arteries to veins
quiz_int:23.r: The faculty answer for this image is the Pacinian corpuscle (p. 1062): deep pressure and vibration, reticular layer (p. 1032, p. 1073).
quiz_int:23.alt: Micrograph of a large round structure built of many thin concentric layers, with fat cells to one side.

quiz_int:24.q: The arrow marks the regularly ridged surface of this hairless skin. What do these surface ridges do?
o: Mark the lines for surgical incision
Tether the skin to the deep fascia
Show tears in the reticular dermis
Show smooth muscle in the dermis
quiz_int:24.r: Dermatoglyphics: papillary ridges are found only on thick skin, each over a dermal papilla; they accentuate tactile sensation and enhance grip (p. 1070, p. 1007). The other options describe Langer's lines, skin creases, striae and wrinkled skin (p. 1074).
quiz_int:24.alt: Low-power section of a curved piece of hairless skin with a wavy surface; yellow arrow on the surface.

quiz_int:25.q: This gland drains into a hair follicle. Which statement about it is correct?
o: It secretes by the merocrine mode
It contains dark cells and clear cells
It is most numerous on palms and soles
It secretes by the holocrine mode
quiz_int:25.r: A sebaceous gland: holocrine secretion of lipid-filled cells produces sebum (p. 1051, p. 1077). It is not under nervous control, is enhanced by androgens from puberty, and is found in thin skin (p. 1077).
quiz_int:25.alt: Micrograph of a lobulated gland made of large pale foamy cells with small dark cells at its edge.

quiz_int:26.q: These coiled glands send their ducts straight to the skin surface. Which nerve fibers stimulate them?
quiz_int:26.r: The faculty answer for this image is eccrine sweat glands (p. 1063). Their innervation is cholinergic sympathetic (p. 1078, p. 1056); apocrine glands receive adrenergic sympathetic fibers (p. 1078).
quiz_int:26.alt: Thick stained section of skin showing coiled glands deep in the dermis with long ducts running up to the surface; yellow arrow on one coil.

quiz_int:28.q: This section is from the axilla. Which statement is true of the glands marked X?
o: They open directly onto the epidermal surface
They contain dark cells but no clear cells
They secrete by the holocrine mode
They are smaller than the glands marked Y
quiz_int:28.r: X marks apocrine sweat glands, which have a larger diameter than eccrine glands (p. 1059, p. 1060). They have only dark cells, secrete by the merocrine mode and open into hair follicles (p. 1058, p. 1078).
quiz_int:28.alt: Micrograph of the deep dermis with two groups of glands: wide tubules with large lumens marked X and small tightly packed tubules marked Y.

quiz_int:29.q: The lecture calls the name of the apocrine sweat gland a misnomer. How do these glands release their product, and where?
o: Merocrine mode, onto the skin surface
Apocrine mode, onto the skin surface
quiz_int:29.r: Apocrine sweat glands secrete via the merocrine (eccrine) mode, not the apocrine mode, and their ducts open into hair follicles (p. 1058, p. 1078).

quiz_int:3.q: Structure B fastens the basal cell to the basement membrane. According to the lecture, which adhesion proteins does this junction use?
quiz_int:3.r: B is a hemidesmosome. The slide pairs desmosomes with cadherins and hemidesmosomes with integrins (p. 1001); laminins belong to the lamina lucida and fibronectin to the fibroreticular lamina (p. 1072).
quiz_int:3.alt: Diagram of the junction between two basal epidermal cells and the tissue beneath them, with structures lettered A to E.

quiz_int:4.q: A patient blisters after the slightest trauma because autoantibodies attack a collagen found nowhere else in the body, and the skin separates below the basal lamina. Which lettered structure is the target?
quiz_int:4.r: Epidermolysis bullosa dystrophica: autoantibodies against type VII collagen, which forms the anchoring fibrils (D) of the dermal-epidermal junction (p. 1072, p. 1025). C is the lamina densa (type IV collagen) and E is a dermal type I collagen fiber.
quiz_int:4.alt: Diagram of the junction between two basal epidermal cells and the tissue beneath them, with structures lettered A to E.

quiz_int:5.q: This skin specimen contains many hair follicles. Compared with skin of the palm, which epidermal layer is absent from this specimen?
quiz_int:5.r: Hair is found in thin skin only (p. 1075). The stratum lucidum is seen only in thick skin; in thin skin the spinosum, granulosum and corneum are thinner but present (p. 1069, p. 1006).
quiz_int:5.alt: Low-power section of skin with many obliquely cut hair follicles.

quiz_int:6.q: This skin section was stained to show elastic fibers in black. The arrow marks one of the thick red bundles that fill the deep dermis. What are these bundles made of?
quiz_int:6.r: The dermis is dense irregular connective tissue of type I collagen bundles with elastic fibers (p. 1029); the reticular layer is 85% type I collagen (p. 1073). Type IV is the lamina densa and type VII the anchoring fibrils (p. 1072).
quiz_int:6.alt: Section of skin with a special stain: epidermis at the top, red bundles and thin black fibers below, yellow arrow on a red bundle.

quiz_int:7.q: These brown-stained cells have branching processes and lie mainly in the stratum spinosum. What is their function?
o: Sense touch at the stratum basale
quiz_int:7.r: The faculty answer for this image is Langerhans cells (p. 1061). They are dendritic cells found mainly in the stratum spinosum that process and present antigens to lymphocytes (p. 1071, p. 1016). Melanocytes sit in the stratum basale.
quiz_int:7.alt: Section of epidermis in which scattered branching cells are stained brown.

quiz_int:9.q: The arrow marks the final product moving out along a process of this epidermal cell. What does this product contain?
quiz_int:9.r: Melanosomes II and III hold tyrosinase plus melanin; the mature melanin granule is a dense collection of melanin with no tyrosinase activity (p. 1010, p. 1070).
quiz_int:9.alt: Diagram of a cell with long processes; pale organelles near the Golgi darken as they move outward, and a yellow arrow marks a black one in a process.

quiz_int_b:1.q: A researcher labels every living cell in a sample of palm epidermis. According to the lecture, which two layers remain unlabeled?
quiz_int_b:1.r: The slide titles the stratum lucidum and stratum corneum the non-living layers, made of squames, with the stratum granulosum as the last living layer beneath them (p. 1005).

quiz_int_b:2.q: Skin biopsies from a very dark-skinned adult and a very fair-skinned adult are compared. According to the lecture, which difference accounts for their skin color?
quiz_int_b:2.r: Skin color depends on the amount of melanin and carotene, not on the number of melanocytes (p. 1015).

quiz_int_b:3.q: This cell of the stratum basale rests on a nerve ending. According to the lecture, what do the arrowed granules in its cytoplasm hold?
quiz_int_b:3.r: This is a Merkel cell, a sensory cell of the stratum basale sitting on a Merkel's disk; its dense core granules are neurotransmitter granules (p. 1018).
quiz_int_b:3.alt: Electron microscope drawing of a rounded cell with a lobed nucleus; a yellow arrow points to a cluster of small dark granules near its base.

quiz_int_b:4.q: This pigmented lesion arose from the melanin-producing cells of the epidermis. According to the lecture, how does this cancer compare with the other two main skin cancers?
o: Most common, causes the most deaths
Most common, causes the fewest deaths
Least common, causes the most deaths
Least common, causes the fewest deaths
quiz_int_b:4.r: Melanoma arises from melanocytes (p. 1020). It makes up under 5% of skin cancers, against over 75% for basal cell and 20% for squamous cell carcinoma, yet causes most skin cancer deaths (p. 1019).
quiz_int_b:4.alt: Clinical photograph of a large, irregular, dark brown skin lesion with uneven color.

quiz_int_b:5.q: The short vessels labeled X join the deep artery directly to the venous plexus, bypassing the capillary loops. According to the lecture, what is their role?
quiz_int_b:5.r: These are arteriovenous shunts (anastomoses), which the slide labels thermoregulation (p. 1031). Scalp cooling uses them to divert blood away from the hair papilla during chemotherapy (p. 1041).
quiz_int_b:5.alt: Line drawing of the blood vessels of the skin, from the capillary loops under the epidermis down to the deep artery and venous plexus, with one set of short vessels labeled X.

quiz_int_b:6.q: The arrow marks the clear layer between the outermost cells of this hair follicle wall and the surrounding dermis. What is this layer?
quiz_int_b:6.r: This is the glassy membrane, which is the basement membrane that separates the hair follicle from the dermis; it lies outside the external root sheath (p. 1044).
quiz_int_b:6.alt: Drawing of a slice through a hair and the wall of its follicle, with the hair at the top and connective tissue at the bottom; a yellow arrow points to a thin clear band near the bottom.

quiz_int_b:7.q: The arrows mark small cells at the outer edge of this gland, whose large pale cells are filled with lipid droplets. What are the arrowed cells?
quiz_int_b:7.r: This is a sebaceous gland, and the small cells at the periphery of each acinus are its stem cells (p. 1050). Myoepithelial, dark and clear cells belong to sweat glands (p. 1053, p. 1058).
quiz_int_b:7.alt: Micrograph of a gland made of rounded lobes of large pale foamy cells surrounded by pink connective tissue; two yellow arrows point to small cells at the edge of the lobes.

quiz_int_b:8.q: These two cells come from the secretory portion of an eccrine sweat gland. Which pairing matches the lecture?
o: A makes sweat; B is antibacterial
A is antibacterial; B makes sweat
A is contractile; B makes sweat
A makes sebum; B is antibacterial
A makes sweat; B is contractile
quiz_int_b:8.r: Cell A is a dark cell, packed with glycoprotein secretory granules (p. 1054) and described as mucoid and antibacterial; cell B is a clear cell, which transports fluid and produces sweat (p. 1053, p. 1054).
quiz_int_b:8.alt: Electron microscope drawings of two gland cells: cell A is narrow and packed with dark granules, cell B is broad with many mitochondria and folded membranes.

brief:
Integument High-Yield Tables (Exam 3)

Integument (Djakiew) was 30/46 (65%) on your September quiz, with hair and nails weakest at 5/11. Page numbers are pages of the combined PDF: slides pp. 991–1066, handout pp. 1067–1078. Everything is from those pages unless labeled (outside the slides).

1. Skin overview, thick versus thin skin (LO 1)

The integument is epidermis, dermis and skin appendages; the hypodermis is not part of it (pp. 994, 1035, 1067).

Part Tissue Origin Page
Epidermis Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium; avascular; free nerve endings Ectoderm 1067
Dermis Dense irregular connective tissue Mesoderm 1029, 1067
Skin appendages Nails, hair, glands: epidermal structures that grow down into the dermis Epidermis 1067, 1074
Hypodermis Fibro-fatty layer; superficial fascia in gross anatomy; not part of the integument 1035, 1073–1074
Number Fact Page
16% Share of body weight; skin is the largest and heaviest organ 1067
1.2–2.2 m2 Surface area 1067
3–5 liters a day Water loss after extensive burns 1067
15–30 days Keratinocyte cycle: mitosis, keratinization, death, exfoliation 1069
4.5% Share of blood volume held in dermal vessels 1073
95% Share of body heat lost through the skin 1073
1.5–2.0 liters an hour Sweat loss in very hot weather 1078

Skin functions: protection, hydrophobic barrier, sensation, thermoregulation, vitamin D synthesis (p. 1067).

Feature Thin skin Thick skin Page
Where Most of the body Palms and soles (volar surfaces of hands and feet) 996, 1067
Hair Present Absent 1067, 1075
Stratum lucidum Absent Present 996, 1006, 1069
Stratum corneum Thin Thicker 996, 1006
Spinosum and granulosum Attenuated Full thickness 1069
Fingerprint ridges No Yes; found only on thick skin 1007, 1070
Special job Resists frictional forces 1067
Meissner's corpuscles Particularly prominent 1073
How to recognize it in an image Thin epidermis; hair follicles and sebaceous glands in the dermis Corneum thicker than the rest of the epidermis; no hair; tall dermal papillae; only sweat glands 1006, 1027

The "how to recognize it" cells in this document are my descriptions of his images; the slides give only labels.

Fingerprint fact (dermatoglyphics) Page
Surface pattern of papillary ridges and grooves 1070
Each ridge lies over a dermal papilla 1070
Accentuate tactile sensation and enhance grip 1070
Unique to each person, identical twins included 1070
Evolution of skin specializations (p. 995) Product
Dermis Dermal scales (fish and amphibians)
Epidermis Epidermal scales (reptiles), then feathers (dinosaurs and birds)
Epidermis Hair and nails (mammals)
Apocrine sweat glands Mammary glands (mammals)

2. Epidermal layers (LO 1)

Thick skin has five layers, listed here from deep to superficial; thin skin lacks the stratum lucidum (pp. 1000, 1006, 1069).

Layer Cells Key content Mitosis How to recognize it in an image Page
Stratum basale (germinativum) Single layer of cuboidal or columnar stem cells Desmosomes to neighbors; hemidesmosomes to the basement membrane Intense One row of crowded dark nuclei sitting on the dermis 1001, 1069
Stratum spinosum Layers of cuboidal or polygonal cells, central nuclei Tonofibrils (bundles of cytokeratin filaments) inserting into desmosomes; active protein synthesis Low Polygonal cells joined by fine "prickles" across a pale gap 1002, 1003, 1065, 1069
Stratum granulosum Flattened cells Keratohyalin granules, lamellar granules, tonofibrils None Flat cells packed with dark granules, just under the pale dead layers 1004, 1069
Stratum lucidum Dead; organelles digested Cytokeratin aggregates in a keratohyalin (filaggrin) matrix None Thin clear band; thick skin only 1005, 1069
Stratum corneum Squames: flat dead cells Mature keratin; abundant intercellular lipid None Outermost flakes with no nuclei 1005, 1069

The prickles of the stratum spinosum are an artifact of tissue shrinkage: cells pull apart but stay joined at their desmosomes (p. 1002). The lucidum and corneum are the non-living layers (p. 1005). Squames are shed as their desmosomes are lost (p. 1069).

Granule of the stratum granulosum Membrane Content Job Page
Keratohyalin granule None Mainly filaggrin, which binds keratin; very basophilic (many phosphate groups) Bundles keratin 1004, 1069
Lamellar granule Membrane coated Lipid sheets Secreted between cells: intercellular cement and a barrier to desiccation 1004, 1069
Function of the epidermis How Page
Abrasion resistance Loose squames of the stratum corneum flake off; tonofibrils and desmosomes of the spinosum 1008, 1069
Physical-chemical barrier Blocks infectious agents and most substances 1008, 1069
Water proofing Intercellular lipid from lamellar granules 1008, 1069
Vitamin D Photo biogenesis with ultraviolet (UV) light 1069
Cytokines Keratinocytes make interleukins 1069

Substances that do cross the barrier: poison ivy resins, nitroglycerin, scopolamine, DMSO (p. 1069).

3. Junctions and the dermal-epidermal junction (LO 1)

Cell-to-cell is desmosome and cadherin; cell-to-basement-membrane is hemidesmosome and integrin (pp. 1001, 1025).

Junction Joins Protein Page
Desmosome Keratinocyte to keratinocyte Cadherins; the core proteins are desmogleins 1001, 1067
Hemidesmosome Basal cell to basement membrane Integrins 1001, 1025

Keratin intermediate filaments anchor to desmosomes; desmosomes give mechanical strength, resist stretching, and are broken and reformed as cells move up (pp. 998, 1067).

Layer of the junction, top to bottom Main component Page
Lamina lucida Laminins 1025, 1072
Lamina densa Type IV collagen 1025, 1072
Fibroreticular lamina Fibronectin 1025, 1072
Anchoring fibrils Type VII collagen; found nowhere else in the body 1025, 1072
Junction fact Detail Page
Shape Epidermal (rete) ridges interlock with dermal papillae: "peg and socket" 1027, 1072
Where it is exaggerated Friction areas such as the soles 1072
Barrier Stops capillaries and large molecules; lets free nerve endings pass 1072
Epidermolysis bullosa dystrophica Autoantibodies against type VII collagen; blisters after the slightest trauma; the split is below the basal lamina 1072

4. The four epidermal cell types (LO 2)

Keratinocytes make up most of the epidermis; the other three are scattered among them (pp. 997, 1067).

Cell Origin Where Job Key fact How to recognize it in an image Page
Keratinocyte Ectoderm Every layer Makes keratin Linked by desmosomes; makes interleukins The ordinary cell of each layer 998, 1067
Melanocyte Neural crest Stratum basale; also hair follicles, eye Makes melanin, which blocks UV and soaks up free radicals Feeds a group of keratinocytes: the epidermal-melanin unit Basal cell body with long processes running up between keratinocytes 1012, 1070
Langerhans cell Bone marrow (from monocytes) Mainly stratum spinosum Antigen presenting cell (APC): processes skin antigens and presents them to lymphocytes No cytokeratin filaments, no desmosomes; travels to lymph nodes by dermal lymphatics Star-shaped (dendritic) cells in the mid epidermis; stained brown on p. 1061 1016, 1061, 1071
Merkel cell Neural crest Stratum basale, especially thick skin Sensory Dense core (neurotransmitter) granules make it an APUD cell; nerve ending at its base is the Merkel's disk Clear basal cell with a nerve ending against its base; small dark granules on the electron-microscope drawing 1018, 1071

Langerhans cells belong to the mononuclear phagocyte system (MPS) (p. 1071). APUD is not spelled out on these pages (outside the slides: amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation). Certain T lymphocytes also home to the epidermis, drawn by keratinocyte interleukins (p. 1071).

Two small conflicts on the Merkel cell. The slide calls it sensory and says it is contacted exclusively by myelinated axons (p. 1018); the handout says its function is unclear (mechanoreceptor or neuro-endocrine) and that free nerve endings form the disk (p. 1071). Answer the handout wording unless a question quotes the slide. The slide also calls its tumor rare (p. 1018).

5. Melanin and skin color (LO 2)

Tyrosinase is active inside the melanosome and gone by the time the granule is mature (pp. 1010, 1070).

Stage Tyrosinase Melanin Page
Tyrosinase synthesis in the rough endoplasmic reticulum, then Golgi Being made None 1010, 1013
Premelanosome Present Not yet 1011
Melanosome (II and III on the slide) Present Being made 1010, 1070
Mature melanin granule No activity Dense 1010, 1070
Granule in a keratinocyte No activity Sits above the nucleus, then is lysed 1013, 1014, 1071
Melanin fact Detail Page
Tyrosinase Copper-containing enzyme 1070
Reaction Tyrosine to melanin in several steps (handout); DOPA to dopaquinone to melanin (slide) 1010, 1070
Melanosome Membrane-bound packet of melanin synthesis 1070
Transfer Mature granules are "injected" into keratinocytes 1071
Who holds more melanin Keratinocytes, not melanocytes 1071
Position in the keratinocyte Supranuclear, on the sunlight side 1014, 1071
Control Genetic, hormonal (MSH/ACTH, estrogen/progesterone), environmental 1071
Type of melanin Color on the slide Color and granule shape in the handout Page
Eumelanin Black Brown-black, ellipsoid 1010, 1071
Pheomelanin Red Red-yellow, round 1010, 1071

The slide and handout colors differ only in wording; use the handout pair (brown-black, red-yellow) unless a question quotes the slide. DOPA, MSH and ACTH are not spelled out on these pages.

Pigment question Answer Page
What sets skin color Melanin and carotene, dermal blood vessels, hemoglobin 1015, 1071
Why skin colors differ Number, size and distribution of melanin granules; not the number of melanocytes 1015, 1071
Albinism Defect in tyrosinase synthesis or activity; no melanin; melanocytes are present 1015, 1071
Tanning, step 1 Existing melanin darkens (physiochemical) 1071
Tanning, step 2 More tyrosinase, so more melanin 1071
Gray hair Hair matrix melanocytes stop making melanin 1046, 1076

6. Dermis, vessels and sensory receptors (LO 3)

The dermis has a thin papillary layer under the epidermis and a thick reticular layer below it (pp. 1026, 1072–1073).

Feature Papillary layer Reticular layer Page
Tissue Loose connective tissue Dense irregular connective tissue 1073
Collagen 10% type III 85% type I 1029, 1073
Elastic fibers Rich Present 1073
Vessels Capillary loops that feed the epidermis Arteriovenous (AV) shunts 1030, 1073
Encapsulated receptor Meissner's corpuscle Pacinian corpuscle 1032, 1073
Other Forms the dermal papillae Arrector pili smooth muscle; leather from animals 1028, 1073

Irregular collagen deposition in the dermis is responsible for wrinkles (p. 1029); sunlight and smoking both wrinkle skin early (pp. 1023, 1036).

Vessel Detail Page
Papillary capillaries Loops; do not enter the epidermis 1031, 1073
Superficial (sub-papillary) plexus Small arterioles and venules 1073
Deep (reticular) plexus At the dermal-hypodermal junction; large arterioles and venules 1073
AV shunts Deep dermis; thermoregulation and blood pressure 1031, 1073
Glomus Highly convoluted AV shunt wrapped in connective tissue; fingertips, ears 1073
Lymphatics Start as blind sacs in dermal papillae 1073
Receptor Where Senses How to recognize it in an image Page
Free nerve ending Extends into the epidermis Not seen on routine sections 1032, 1073
Merkel's cell and disk Stratum basale Sensory Basal cell with a nerve ending at its base 1018, 1032
Meissner's corpuscle Dermal papilla (papillary layer); fingertips, thick skin Light touch Oval stack of flattened cells filling a dermal papilla 1032, 1033, 1073
Pacinian corpuscle Reticular layer; palms, soles, genitalia Deep pressure and vibration Large round body of concentric layers, like a cut onion 1032, 1034, 1062, 1073
Peritrichial nerve endings Around the hair follicle Touch 1076

Efferent nerves to the skin are sympathetic only (p. 1073).

Hypodermis and skin lines Detail Page
Hypodermis Anchors skin loosely; fat is a cushion, insulator and energy store 1073–1074
Lines of cleavage (Langer's lines) Parallel collagen bundles; cut parallel to them for the best scar 1074
Skin creases Skin tethered to deep fascia so it folds 1074
Wrinkled skin of scrotum, areola Smooth muscle in the reticular dermis 1074
Striae (stretch marks) Torn reticular dermis repaired by scar 1074

7. Nails (LO 3)

Only the nail matrix makes the nail; the nail bed just supports it (p. 1074).

Part What it is Job How to recognize it in an image Page
Nail plate (and root) Hard plate of keratinized cells; like stratum corneum but harder The plate on top; its free edge overhangs the fingertip 1038, 1074
Nail matrix Epidermis at the base of the nail root Forms the nail Deepest, proximal end, buried under the skin fold 1038, 1074
Nail bed Strata basale and spinosum only Supports the plate; does not form it Thin epithelium directly under the plate 1038, 1074
Eponychium (cuticle) Reflected stratum corneum along the nail folds Protects the nail matrix from infection Lip of skin lying on the proximal plate 1038, 1074
Hyponychium Thickened stratum corneum under the free edge Protects the nail bed from infection Under the free edge, at the fingertip 1038, 1074
Lunula White opaque crescent at the proximal end Marks the distal end of the matrix Crescent on the surface view 1038, 1075

Nails form like hairs but as plates rather than cylinders (p. 1074). The clear plate and thin bed are a window on the color and oxygen of the blood below (p. 1075).

8. Hair (LO 3)

The follicle is an epidermal invagination, and its one dermal part is the hair papilla (pp. 1039, 1040, 1075).

Follicle part What it is Key fact How to recognize it in an image Page
